input:
A countercurrent exchanger is used to cool a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C, with cooling water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 65 °C, and the quantity required for sizing calculations of this kind is the log-mean temperature difference, denoted $\Delta T_{lm}$, which accounts for the fact that the local temperature difference between the two streams is not the same at the two ends of the exchanger. At the end where the water leaves, the difference between the streams is 95 K, while at the end where the water enters, the difference is 80 K, and the appropriate mean of these two terminal differences, for an exchanger of this type, is given by the relation $$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$ in which the two terminal differences appear in the numerator and inside the logarithm. Evaluating the relation with the terminal differences stated above gives the log-mean temperature difference as 87.3 K. It is worth noting that this value rests on particular assumptions: the log-mean value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream, and where those conditions do not hold the single log-mean figure no longer describes the exchanger in the same way.

The arithmetic mean of the two terminal differences would not serve the same purpose. Along the length of the exchanger, the local difference changes from one end to the other, and the contribution of each part of the surface to the heat transferred depends on the local difference at that part, so a mean that weights the two ends in the logarithmic way set out above is the mean that matches how the exchanger actually transfers heat. The resulting figure is then the temperature difference that, together with the surface area and the overall coefficient, sets the duty of the exchanger, which is why the log-mean value, rather than either terminal difference on its own, is the quantity carried into sizing work.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 65 °C. The local temperature difference between the streams differs at the two ends of the exchanger, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is the mean used for sizing. At the end where the water leaves, the terminal difference is 95 K. At the end where the water enters, the terminal difference is 80 K. The log-mean temperature difference is calculated from the two terminal differences by $$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$ Substitution of the two terminal differences gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ as 87.3 K. The value lies between the two terminal differences. The log-mean value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream. Where the overall coefficient varies along the exchanger, or where a stream changes phase, a single log-mean figure does not describe the exchanger in the same way, and the exchanger is treated in sections instead.

An arithmetic mean of the two terminal differences does not serve the same purpose. The local difference changes along the length of the exchanger. Each part of the surface transfers heat in proportion to the local difference at that part. The logarithmic mean weights the two ends in the way the surface actually transfers heat. The log-mean temperature difference then sets the duty of the exchanger together with the surface area and the overall coefficient. The two assumptions mark the scope of the single figure. A constant overall coefficient means one value is used along the whole length. No phase change means each stream changes temperature by sensible heat alone from one end to the other, and the two terminal differences describe the ends completely.
